Why Bitcoiners and CrowdHealth Members Think Alike

Fewer middlemen, direct payment, numbers you can check, and a long view.

New to CrowdHealth? Start with my CrowdHealth guide and every post, grouped by question.

In short

People who save in bitcoin and people who use CrowdHealth tend to share four habits: they cut out the middleman, they pay directly, they like numbers they can check themselves, and they think in years, not months. That's why so many bitcoiners end up on CrowdHealth, and why CrowdHealth runs a bitcoin savings program. It doesn't mean one fits everybody who likes the other.

In 2022 my family of four canceled an expensive insurance plan and joined CrowdHealth. No regrets. I also buy bitcoin every week on River. For a while I thought those were two separate parts of my life, like peanut butter and a power drill. Then I noticed how many people I talk to do both. It isn't a coincidence. It's the same way of thinking, pointed at two different problems.

Habit 1: Cut out the middleman

CrowdHealth's member guide says it plainly: members use healthcare as self-pay patients, "cutting out the health insurance middleman." You deal with the doctor. The crowd helps with the big bills. You pick any doctor you want.

Bitcoin works the same way with money. You can hold it yourself, with no bank in between. I buy on River with its ForceField security setting turned on, and auto-withdrawal moves my bitcoin to a hardware wallet I control. ForceField is explained in bitcoin scams and the lock I use. I explain why that matters in not your keys.

Think of the farmers market. You hand the farmer your money and get the tomatoes. No warehouse, no distributor, no grocery chain taking a cut along the way. Fewer hands in the middle means fewer people getting paid to slow things down.

Habit 2: Pay directly, and ask the price

CrowdHealth members ask for the cash price. The member guide says self-pay discounts run from 25% to 85% off normal billed charges. That's the whole idea behind the cash price secret.

Bitcoiners like paying directly, too. You can send it to anyone without asking a bank for permission or waiting days for it to clear.

Both groups are comfortable with a little more responsibility in exchange for fewer surprises from someone else's fine print.

Habit 3: Don't trust, check

This is the one I love most.

CrowdHealth publishes its monthly cost history. You can see that in 2026 a single member under 55 paid between $125 and $165 a month, before card fees. It also publishes Transparency Files on how bills got funded. CrowdHealth says 99.9% of eligible bills have been funded to date, and its results page lets you look for yourself. I dig into those in where the crowd's money goes.

River publishes a proof of reserves every month. Its October 6, 2026 proof showed 33,404.73 bitcoin in assets against 33,332.42 bitcoin owed to customers. You can even look up your own balance on the list. More on that in proof of reserves, explained.

Your insurance company doesn't show you what last month's claims looked like. Your bank doesn't show you its vault. These two do. Bitcoiners have a saying for this: don't trust, verify.

Habit 4: Think in decades

Bitcoin savers buy a little at a time and leave it alone. I don't try to time the price. I wrote about why in why I don't try to time the price.

CrowdHealth leans the same direction with your health. There's an annual wellness feature, quarterly specials on tests like DEXA scans and fasting insulin, and a new Longevity Discount of up to 20% off the monthly contribution for passing certain health tests. And CrowdHealth makes its money from the flat advocacy fee, not a cut of the bills, so it isn't rewarded when you're sick.

Both reward patience over the quick fix. If the CrowdHealth side appeals to you, you can join with my code NORMAL (opens in a new tab) and get your first 3 months at $99 a month per member.

The honest part

Sharing habits doesn't mean sharing risks. They're very different.

  • CrowdHealth isn't insurance. It's healthcare crowdfunding, and there's no legal promise a bill gets funded. You're still responsible for your own bills.
  • Bitcoin's price swings hard. It can drop a lot and stay down for years. It isn't where my $500 member commitment lives. That stays in cash, and I explain why in why my $500 cushion lives in cash.
  • Doing it yourself is work. Self-pay means paperwork. Self-custody means guarding your keys. Neither one is for someone who wants to hand everything off.

If you like one, the other might fit you. It might not. Look at each one on its own.

Questions I get about this

Do I have to own bitcoin to join CrowdHealth?

No. You pay CrowdHealth in dollars like anyone else. The bitcoin piece is optional. CrowdHealth's Fold+ program can sweep your unused crowdfunding into bitcoin, which I cover in CrowdHealth's bitcoin savings program.

Can I pay medical bills with bitcoin?

Some providers might take it, but most want dollars. I keep bitcoin as long-term savings and pay bills from cash. Selling bitcoin to pay a bill can also be a taxable event, so talk to a tax pro.

Is this a political thing?

Not for me. It's a math and paperwork thing. I like seeing the numbers, and I like fewer people standing between me and my money.
